title: The Knowledge Is Secure What Next
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Once students can retrieve key facts, Castelino asks what comes next and answers that it is building and practising connections between them. She describes a structured extended-answer routine used at the end of a unit in GCSE science: students read the question, split their mini-whiteboard, list key terms, write a short note on each, check with a partner using Turn and Talk, then write the full response while the teacher scans and uses Show Call under the visualiser. She notes that the knowledge needed must be secure first and that classroom culture must support the technique. Her observation is that extended-writing practice often focuses on command words instead of activating the knowledge the question requires. It is Learning & Curriculum because it is pedagogy for knowledge and writing.
points: After retrieval is secure, the next step is explicitly teaching students to link facts into a bigger picture.
Listing key terms and a brief note on each before answering lets students gather the needed knowledge and lets the teacher check it quickly.
Turn and Talk, then Show Call under the visualiser, give layered feedback before and after students write their full response.
Extended writing practice works only when the knowledge to be activated is already secure.
quotes: The knowledge is secure, what next? It won’t come as a surprise that I think the next step involves building connections and, crucially, showing students how to do this and incorporating practice of this in lessons.

In this post, I want to focus on getting students to explain concepts at length. I am not talking about goal-free tasks, although they are useful too, but tasks that get students to think deeply about a concept and to view the bigger picture, with a bit more structure. And instead of me questioning them slowly, this is a way to get students to see how the parts fit into the whole by themselves.

Of course, when you have a large class, it is possible to miss some detail in the answers on MWBs/books as you walk and scan. Having the bullet points initially makes it easier to scan but to add a layer where students can feel confident about what they have written, the next step helps.

I am finding my students are more confident and comfortable with extended writing due to these questions. A lot of the time when I hear about extended writing practice, the focus tends to be on command words rather than activating the relevant knowledge that is needed to answer the question.
Using this method, I am getting my students to practise extended writing but within context. And it only works if the knowledge needed to be activated is first secure.
